p.src: Now Pang Tong and Fa Zheng urged Xuande to kill Liu Zhang at the banquet, saying that the Western Riverlands would then be his for the taking. Xuande said, “I have only just entered Shu, and have not yet established goodwill or trust. This must never be done.” The two pressed him again and again, but Xuande would not consent. The next day he again feasted with Liu Zhang in the city. They spoke freely of their innermost feelings and grew exceedingly close. When the wine had brought them to half-drunkenness, Pang Tong and Fa Zheng conferred, saying, “Matters have come this far; our lord can no longer have his way.” They ordered Wei Yan to enter the hall and perform a sword dance, intending him to seize the moment and kill Liu Zhang. Wei Yan drew his sword, stepped forward, and said, “There is no entertainment at this feast. Allow me to perform a sword dance for your amusement.” Pang Tong summoned the warriors inside and arrayed them below the hall, waiting only for Wei Yan to strike. Liu Zhang’s generals saw Wei Yan dancing with his sword before the feast, and also saw the warriors below the steps gripping their sword hilts and staring into the hall. Zhang Ren, an officer of Liu Zhang’s staff, likewise drew his sword and danced, saying, “A sword dance must have a partner. I shall dance with General Wei.”

p.src: The two danced opposite each other before the feast. Wei Yan glanced at Liu Feng, who also drew his sword and joined the dance. Then Liu Gui, Leng Bao, and Deng Xian each drew their swords and came forward, saying, “Let us all dance together to add to the merriment.” Greatly alarmed, Xuande snatched a sword from one of his attendants, stood up at the table, and said, “We brothers have met to drink our fill, with neither suspicion nor mistrust between us. This is no Banquet at Hong Gate—what need is there for sword dancing? Anyone who does not cast down his sword shall be beheaded at once!” Liu Zhang also rebuked them, saying, “Why bear blades when brothers are gathered together?” He ordered all the guards to remove their swords. Amid much confusion, they all descended from the hall. Xuande summoned the officers and soldiers back onto the dais, bestowed wine upon them, and said, “We two brothers are blood kin of the same clan and are consulting together on great affairs. Neither of us harbors a divided heart. You must not be suspicious.” The generals all bowed and thanked him. Liu Zhang took Xuande’s hand and wept, saying, “Elder brother, I swear I shall never forget your kindness!” The two drank merrily until evening, then parted. Upon returning to camp, Xuande reproached Pang Tong: “Why did you gentlemen seek to entrap me in an unrighteous deed? Never attempt such a thing again.” Pang Tong withdrew with a sigh.

p.src: Now when Liu Zhang returned to his camp, Liu Gui and the others said, “My lord, did you see what happened at today’s banquet? It would be best to return early and avoid future trouble.” Liu Zhang said, “My elder brother Liu Xuande is not like other men.” The generals said, “Even if Xuande himself has no such intention, all his subordinates wish to annex the Western Riverlands in pursuit of wealth and rank.” Liu Zhang said, “Do not sow discord between us brothers.” He would not listen, and spent each day conversing happily with Xuande.

p.src: Suddenly a report arrived that Zhang Lu had marshaled his troops and was about to attack Jiameng Pass. Liu Zhang asked Xuande to go and resist him. Xuande readily agreed and that very day led his own troops toward Jiameng Pass. The generals urged Liu Zhang to have senior commanders guard every strategic pass closely, lest Xuande’s army revolt. At first Liu Zhang refused, but after everyone pressed him earnestly, he ordered Yang Huai and Gao Pei, the commanders of Baishui, to guard Fushui Pass. Liu Zhang himself returned to Chengdu. On reaching Jiameng Pass, Xuande imposed strict discipline on his soldiers and dispensed favors widely, thereby winning the people’s hearts.

p.src: Spies soon carried the news to Eastern Wu. Sun Quan, Marquis of Wu, assembled his civil and military officials for consultation. Gu Yong stepped forward and said, “Liu Bei has divided his forces and gone far away across perilous mountains; he cannot easily return. Why not send a force first to block the mouth of the river into Sichuan and cut off his route of retreat, then muster all the troops of Eastern Wu and take Jing and Xiang in a single assault? This is an opportunity that must not be lost.” Sun Quan said, “An excellent plan!”

p.src: While they were still deliberating, someone suddenly strode out from behind a screen and shouted, “Whoever proposed this plan deserves to be beheaded! Do you mean to take my daughter’s life?” Everyone looked in astonishment: it was the Dowager Lady of Wu. The Dowager said angrily, “I have but one daughter in all the world, and she is married to Liu Bei. If you now raise troops, what will become of her life?” Then she rebuked Sun Quan: “You hold the inheritance of your father and elder brother and rule eighty-one prefectures, yet still you are not satisfied! You covet a petty gain and give no thought to your own flesh and blood!” Sun Quan repeatedly assented and replied, “How could I dare disobey my honored mother’s instruction?” He then angrily dismissed the officials. The Dowager withdrew, still seething with anger. Standing beneath the veranda, Sun Quan thought to himself, “If this opportunity is lost, when shall I ever obtain Jing and Xiang?”

p.src: As he pondered in silence, Zhang Zhao entered and asked, “My lord, what troubles and perplexes you?” Sun Quan said, “I was thinking about what just occurred.” Zhang Zhao said, “That is easily resolved. Send one trusted officer with only five hundred soldiers to slip into Jingzhou and deliver a secret letter to the Lady, saying only that the Dowager is gravely ill and longs to see her own daughter. Have the Lady return to Eastern Wu that very night. Xuande has only one son in all his life; have her bring him along. Xuande will then surely exchange Jingzhou for A’dou. If he does not, you may freely resort to arms—what obstacle would remain?” Sun Quan said, “An excellent plan! I have a man named Zhou Shan, who is exceptionally daring; from childhood he has known how to slip through houses and enter private chambers, and often accompanied my elder brother. He can be sent on this mission.” Zhang Zhao said, “Be certain that nothing leaks out. Order him to depart at once.”

p.src: Sun Quan therefore secretly dispatched Zhou Shan with five hundred men, disguised as traveling merchants and divided among five boats; he also forged an official letter of state to meet any questioning. Weapons were concealed inside the boats. Having received his orders, Zhou Shan traveled by water toward Jingzhou. The boats moored by the river. Zhou Shan entered Jingzhou alone and had the gatekeeper announce him to Lady Sun. The Lady ordered Zhou Shan admitted, and he presented the secret letter. When the Lady read that the Dowager was gravely ill, she burst into tears and anxiously questioned him. Zhou Shan bowed and reported, “The Dowager is desperately ill and thinks of nothing but you, my lady, from morning till night. If you are late in going, I fear you may not see her alive. She also bids you bring A’dou so that she may see him once.” The Lady said, “The Imperial Uncle has led the army far away. If I am to return now, I must send someone to inform the Military Advisor before I can leave.” Zhou Shan said, “What if the Military Advisor replies, ‘We must inform the Imperial Uncle and await his answer before you may board the boat’?” The Lady said, “If I leave without taking my farewell, I fear someone may try to stop me.” Zhou Shan said, “The boats have already been made ready on the great river. I beg you, my lady, to enter your carriage and leave the city this very moment.” How could Lady Sun remain calm upon hearing that her mother was near death? She placed the seven-year-old A’dou in her carriage; with more than thirty attendants following, each armed with sword or saber, she mounted and left Jingzhou, then went straight to the riverbank and boarded the boat. By the time the people at the residence sought to report the matter, Lady Sun had already reached Shatou Town and boarded the boat.

p.src: Just as Zhou Shan was about to set sail, someone on the bank shouted, “Do not cast off yet! Allow me to bid the Lady farewell!” They looked and saw that it was Zhao Yun. Zhao Yun had just returned from patrol when he heard the news. Startled, he took only four or five riders and raced along the riverbank like a whirlwind. Holding a long halberd, Zhou Shan shouted, “Who are you, to dare obstruct our mistress?” He ordered the soldiers to cast off together. Each brought out his weapon and took position on the boats. With a fair wind and swift current, all the boats sped downstream. Zhao Yun pursued along the bank, shouting, “The Lady may go as she pleases. I ask only to report one matter to her.”

p.src: Zhou Shan ignored him and merely urged the boat onward at full speed. Zhao Yun pursued them for more than ten li along the river, when he suddenly saw a fishing boat moored at an angle by the riverbank. Zhao Yun abandoned his horse, took up his spear, and leapt into the fishing boat. With only two men rowing, he set out and pursued the great ship carrying the Lady. Zhou Shan ordered the soldiers to loose their arrows. Zhao Yun swept them aside with his spear, and the arrows fell one after another into the water. When little more than a zhang separated the boats, the soldiers of Wu thrust wildly at him with their spears. Zhao Yun cast down his spear in the small boat, drew the Blue Steel Sword from his side, beat aside the stabbing spears, and sprang toward the Wu vessel, landing at once upon the great ship. The soldiers of Wu all recoiled in terror.

p.src: Zhao Yun entered the cabin and saw the Lady holding A-Dou in her arms. She shouted at him, “Why are you so insolent?” Zhao Yun sheathed his sword, saluted, and said, “My Lady, where do you intend to go? Why did you not have the Military Adviser informed?” The Lady replied, “My mother is gravely ill, and there was no time to send word.” Zhao Yun said, “If my Lady is going to visit the sick, why are you taking the young lord with you?” The Lady replied, “A-Dou is my son. If he remained in Jingzhou, there would be no one to care for him.” Zhao Yun said, “My Lady, you are mistaken. My lord has no other flesh and blood in all the world but this child. I rescued him from an army of a million at Changban Slope in Dangyang. What reason can there be for my Lady to carry him away today?” The Lady angrily replied, “You are merely a fighting man under my husband’s command. How dare you meddle in my family affairs!” Zhao Yun said, “If my Lady wishes to go, then go—but leave the young lord behind.” The Lady cried, “You have forced your way aboard in mid-journey; you must be plotting rebellion!” Zhao Yun replied, “Unless you leave the young lord behind, even if I must die ten thousand deaths, I dare not let my Lady depart.”

p.src: The Lady ordered her maids to seize him, but Zhao Yun pushed them down, snatched A-Dou from her arms, and carried him out to the bow. He wished to bring the vessel alongside the bank, but had no one to help him; he wished to use force, but feared that it would violate what was right. Thus he could neither advance nor retreat. The Lady ordered her maids to take back A-Dou. Zhao Yun held A-Dou firmly in one arm and brandished his sword with the other, so no one dared approach. At the stern, Zhou Shan held fast to the tiller and cared only to send the ship downstream. With the wind behind them and the current swift, they headed into midstream. One hand alone cannot clap: Zhao Yun could do no more than protect A-Dou, so how could he bring the vessel to shore?

p.src: After reading the letter, Sun Quan wept and said to those assembled, “Zhang Zigang urged me to move my residence to Moling. How can I refuse to follow his counsel?” He immediately ordered the seat of government moved to Jianye and had Stone City constructed. Lü Meng came forward and said, “Since Cao Cao’s army is approaching, we should build a fortified dock at the mouth of the Ruxu River to resist him.” The other generals all said, “We go ashore to strike the enemy and board our ships barefoot. What need is there to build a fortress?” Lü Meng replied, “Weapons may prove keen or dull, and victory in battle is never certain. If we suddenly encounter the enemy and their infantry and cavalry press us hard, men will not even have time to reach the water—how could they board the ships?” Sun Quan said, “‘He who gives no thought to distant troubles will soon face troubles close at hand.’ Ziming’s foresight is indeed far-reaching.” He therefore assigned tens of thousands of troops to construct the Ruxu fortification. They labored day and night and completed it by the appointed date.

They labored day and night and completed it by the appointed date.

p.src: Meanwhile, in the capital Xu, Cao Cao’s authority and influence grew greater with each passing day. Chief Clerk Dong Zhao came forward and said, “Since ancient times, no subject has ever rendered achievements equal to those of the Prime Minister. Not even the Duke of Zhou or Lü Wang could surpass you. For more than thirty years you have braved wind and rain, swept away every villain, rid the people of their afflictions, and enabled the house of Han to endure. How can you remain ranked together with ordinary ministers? You should receive the rank of Duke of Wei and be granted the Nine Bestowments to proclaim your merit and virtue.” And what, you may ask, were those “Nine Bestowments”?

p.src: Palace Attendant Xun Yu said, “That must not be. The Prime Minister originally raised a righteous army to support and restore the house of Han. He should uphold a loyal and steadfast purpose and preserve the virtue of humility and restraint. A gentleman cares for others by guiding them toward virtue. This proposal is improper.” At these words, Cao Cao’s expression changed abruptly with anger. Dong Zhao said, “How can the hopes of the multitude be thwarted by a single man?” He then submitted a memorial requesting that Cao Cao be elevated to Duke of Wei and granted the Nine Bestowments. Xun Yu sighed, “I never thought I would live to see such a thing!”

p.src: When Cao Cao heard of this, he deeply resented Xun Yu, believing that he refused to support him. In the tenth month of winter in the seventeenth year of Jian’an, Cao Cao raised an army and marched south toward the Yangzi, ordering Xun Yu to accompany him. Xun Yu already knew that Cao Cao intended to kill him, so he pleaded illness and remained at Shouchun. Suddenly, Cao Cao sent a man bearing a box of food. The box bore a seal written in Cao Cao’s own hand. When Xun Yu opened it, there was nothing inside. Understanding Cao Cao’s meaning, Xun Yu took poison and died. He was fifty years old. p.src: Now Cao Cao’s great army reached Ruxu. He first dispatched Cao Hong with thirty thousand armored cavalry to scout as far as the riverbank. Cao Hong returned and reported, “Looking from afar, I saw countless banners all along the river, but could not tell where the troops were concentrated.” Cao Cao remained uneasy, so he personally led his forces forward and deployed them in battle formation at the mouth of the Ruxu. With more than a hundred men, Cao Cao ascended a hillside and gazed into the distance at the warships, each division arrayed in proper order. Their banners displayed the five colors, and their weapons gleamed brightly. On the great ship in the center, beneath a green silk parasol, sat Sun Quan. His civil and military officers stood in attendance on either side. Pointing with his whip, Cao Cao said, “If one has a son, he should be like Sun Zhongmou! The sons of Liu Jingsheng are no more than swine and curs!”

p.src: Suddenly there came a great sound, and all the southern ships sped forward together. Another force emerged from the Ruxu stockade and threw Cao Cao's troops into disorder. Cao Cao's men turned and fled; no amount of shouting could halt them. Suddenly several hundred horsemen pursued them to the foot of the hill, led by a rider with blue eyes and a purple beard. They recognized him as none other than Sun Quan. Sun Quan himself led a cavalry unit against Cao Cao. Cao Cao was greatly alarmed and was just turning his horse when the Eastern Wu generals Han Dang and Zhou Tai charged straight at him. Behind Cao Cao, Xu Chu spurred forward, brandishing his saber, and held off the two generals, allowing Cao Cao to escape back to camp. Xu Chu fought the two generals for thirty bouts before returning. Back at camp, Cao Cao richly rewarded Xu Chu and berated his generals: “You retreated before engaging the enemy and blunted the vigor of my army! If this happens again, every one of you will be beheaded!”

p.src: That night, around the third watch, a tremendous clamor suddenly arose outside the camp. Cao Cao hastily mounted and saw fires rising on every side: the Wu troops had broken into the main camp. The fighting continued until dawn, when Cao Cao's army withdrew more than fifty li and made camp. Cao Cao, deeply troubled, idly read a treatise on war. Cheng Yu said, “Since the Prime Minister understands the art of war, surely you know that ‘in war, speed is of the essence’? When you raised this army, you delayed for far too long, and thus Sun Quan had time to prepare. He has built a stockade enclosing the mouth of the Ruxu River, and it is difficult to attack. We would do better to withdraw for now and return to the capital at Xu, there to devise a better plan.”

p.src: Cao Cao made no reply. Cheng Yu withdrew. Cao Cao leaned upon his desk and fell asleep. Suddenly he heard the surging roar of the tide, like ten thousand horses racing together. He looked quickly and saw a red sun emerging from the great river, its radiance dazzling his eyes; when he looked up at the sky, two more suns shone opposite it. Suddenly the red sun in the middle of the river flew straight upward and fell among the hills before the camp with a thunderous crash. He awoke with a start and found that he had been dreaming in his tent. The soldiers outside the tent reported that it was noon. Cao Cao ordered horses prepared and rode straight out of camp with more than fifty horsemen. He reached the hill beside which the sun had fallen in his dream, and while he was looking about, a body of horsemen suddenly appeared, led by a man in a golden helmet and golden armor. Cao Cao looked and saw that it was Sun Quan.

p.src: Seeing Cao Cao approach, Sun Quan showed no alarm. He reined in his horse atop the hill, pointed his whip at Cao Cao, and said, “Prime Minister, you command the Central Plain and have attained the height of wealth and honor. Why does your greed remain unsatisfied, that you come again to invade my lands south of the Yangtze?” Cao Cao replied, “You are a subject, yet you do not honor the imperial house. I have come expressly to punish you under the Son of Heaven's decree!” Sun Quan laughed. “Are you not ashamed to utter such words? Does not everyone under heaven know that you hold the Son of Heaven hostage to command the feudal lords? It is not that I fail to honor the Han dynasty; I seek precisely to punish you and set the realm to rights!”

p.src: Cao Cao flew into a rage and ordered his generals to climb the hill and seize Sun Quan. Suddenly a drum sounded, and two strong forces emerged from behind the hill: Han Dang and Zhou Tai on the right, and Chen Wu and Pan Zhang on the left. The four generals led three thousand archers and crossbowmen in a volley, and arrows fell like rain. Cao Cao hurriedly led his generals back in retreat. The four generals pursued fiercely from behind. Halfway back, Xu Chu arrived with the Tiger Guard, held off the pursuers, and rescued Cao Cao. The Wu troops sang their victory songs together and returned to Ruxu.

p.src: Returning to camp, Cao Cao reflected, “Sun Quan is no ordinary man. The omen of the red sun means that in time he will surely become an emperor.” Thereafter he began to consider withdrawing his army. Yet he feared the ridicule of Eastern Wu and could not decide whether to advance or retreat. The two sides remained locked in opposition for more than another month and fought several battles, with victory passing back and forth. At last, in the first month of the following year, continuous spring rains filled every creek and inlet, and the soldiers, often mired in mud and water, suffered extraordinary hardship. Cao Cao was greatly worried. That day, he was in camp conferring with his advisers. Some urged him to withdraw the army; others said that now the spring weather was warm, it was the very time to maintain the standoff, and they must not retreat. Cao Cao hesitated, unable to decide. Suddenly it was reported that an envoy from Eastern Wu had arrived bearing a letter. Cao Cao opened it and read. The letter said in brief: “I and the Prime Minister are both ministers of the Han dynasty. Yet instead of considering how to serve the state and bring peace to the people, the Prime Minister recklessly takes up arms and cruelly destroys living beings. Is this the conduct of a benevolent man? The spring waters are now beginning to rise; you should depart at once. If you do not, the calamity of Red Cliffs will befall you again. You would do well to consider this yourself.”

p.src: On the back of the letter two further lines were inscribed: “Until you die, I shall know no peace.” When Cao Cao had finished reading, he laughed heartily and said, “Sun Zhongmou does not deceive me.” He richly rewarded the envoy and then ordered the army home. He commanded Zhu Guang, Governor of Lujiang, to defend Wan, while he personally led the main army back to Xuchang. Sun Quan likewise withdrew his army to Moling. Sun Quan conferred with his generals: “Though Cao Cao has gone north, Liu Bei is still at Jiameng Pass and has not returned. Why not use the troops that resisted Cao Cao to seize Jingzhou?” Zhang Zhao offered a plan: “We should not yet mobilize the army. I have a plan that will prevent Liu Bei from ever returning to Jingzhou.” Thus it was:
